name: Student Self Assessment
title: Student Self Assessment
answer: Student self assessment is when students judge their own work against clear criteria and set their own goals for improvement, rather than waiting for a teacher or a tool to tell them what to fix. It matters because students who understand their own progress can take charge of their learning, and the text reports that goal setting produced the largest gains in revision in one study of upper secondary students. The teacher's role shifts to reviewing those goals and helping students pursue them.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: Self assessment gives students a way to understand their own progress so they can take charge of their learning. It asks them to measure their work against criteria that are clear to them, name what they did well, and choose one thing to improve. The problem it solves is that a student with no view of their own progress has no reason to revise, while a specific goal gives them one. The goal belongs to the student, not to the tool or the teacher, and that ownership is what makes the improvement meaningful. Over time the practice builds the student's own judgment rather than dependence on an outside verdict.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text names one grade band explicitly, upper secondary students, in the study described below, and otherwise describes the routine in general terms. A school configured tool can coach a student through self assessment by asking them to compare their work with a rubric, identify strengths, and name one thing to improve. The student sets the goal, not the tool, and the teacher reviews the goals and helps students pursue them. The same sequence can run with a paper rubric and a written goal, with the teacher checking both. Self assessment is also named as a key part of the gradual handoff of learning decisions to students.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers one study as its evidence. In a study with 345 upper secondary students, goal setting based on automated scores produced the largest gains in revision (Jansen et al., 2024). The text's own explanation of that finding is that students with specific goals had a reason to improve. The text does not attach a separate evidence label to this idea beyond reporting that study, and it gives no further figures or findings.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Self assessment is not accurate at the start. Students may rate their work too high or too low, and comparing their ratings with the teacher's is what helps them calibrate. The judgment that matters stays with the student, because the student sets the goal and the tool does not set it for them. The teacher keeps the responsibility for reviewing the goals and helping students pursue them, so the practice does not take the teacher out of the loop. The text frames self assessment as something that builds judgment over time, which means early ratings are a starting point rather than a verdict.
